Notes towards a planting plan for the north bed

The north bed gets four hours of direct sun in midsummer and none at all
between November and February. Everything that has failed there so far failed
for the same reason, which is that it was chosen from a catalogue photograph
taken in a garden facing the other way.

What survives is instructive. The hellebores have spread without being asked.
Two ferns put in as an afterthought are now the largest things in the bed. The
epimedium has done nothing visible for three years and is evidently perfectly
happy. What died: every salvia, the lavender, both attempts at a rose, and a
euphorbia that looked robust enough to manage.

The pattern is obvious in retrospect. Plants adapted to woodland floor
conditions are thriving in what is, functionally, a woodland floor. Plants
adapted to open Mediterranean hillsides are not, and no amount of feeding or
drainage will persuade them otherwise, because the limiting factor is light and
light cannot be amended into the soil.

So the plan is to stop fighting it. Ferns, hellebores, epimedium, and pulmonaria
for early colour, with snowdrops and wood anemone underneath for the weeks when
nothing above ground is doing anything. Texture rather than flower, since flower
is what the light will not support.

The one indulgence is a hydrangea in the corner that catches the late afternoon.
It will probably be fine, and if it is not, that will at least be a mistake made
knowingly rather than by copying a photograph.
